Title: Automating HPC Software Compilation, Deployment, and Error Resolution through an LLM-based Multi-Agent System

Abstract
High-performance computing (HPC) systems rely on complex soft-
ware configurations that are traditionally managed through manual
processes, leading to inefficiencies and increased risk of errors. In
this paper, we present an LLM-based multi-agent system designed to
automate the compilation, deployment, and error resolution of HPC
software. Our approach leverages state-of-the-art language models
to generate, refine, and iteratively improve build scripts, thereby
reducing reliance on static documentation and manual intervention.
Extensive experiments on a benchmark cluster demonstrate a 97%
success rate in autonomously building over 200 commonly used
HPC software packages. Moreover, our agents effectively identify
and rectify build and test failures and provide detailed descriptions
with actionable recommendations when manual intervention is
required. This advancement significantly reduces administrative
overhead, enabling HPC administrators to reallocate resources to
other critical tasks and paving the way for more resilient and effi-
cient system operations.

1
Introduction
High-performance computing (HPC) systems form the backbone
of scientific research and engineering innovation [8]. They en-
able intricate simulations, detailed data analyses, and compute-
intensive operations that are essential across disciplines such as
climate modeling [2], bioinformatics [7], and particle physics [12].
At the core of these systems lies a complex ecosystem of software
modules—ranging from compilers to specialized libraries and appli-
cations—that must work together. Despite the critical importance of
these components, the traditional processes for configuring, compil-
ing, deploying, and troubleshooting these software modules remain
predominantly manual and prone to error [29]. The manual nature
of these tasks is a significant problem. HPC system administrators
and engineers must often navigate convoluted dependency chains,
select correct versions, and tailor configurations to the unique re-
quirements of each HPC application. Each step typically relies on
static documentation or community-based support, which can be
outdated or insufficiently detailed [5]. These approaches frequently
result in delays, misconfigurations, and operational bottlenecks, ul-
timately impeding system performance and compromising overall
security. Also, the lack of automated error resolution means that
when issues arise, they can stall critical computational workflows
or, worse, lead to inconsistent deployment practices [1].
Automating the software installation process in HPC environ-
ments is both timely and essential. Modern HPC systems contin-
ually evolve, facing rapid increases in software complexity and
stricter performance requirements. With an ever-growing number
of tools and libraries, ensuring that each component is correctly
configured becomes more challenging. Manual processes not only
demand extensive time and specialized expertise but also heighten
the risk of vulnerabilities when outdated or misconfigured software
goes unchecked. An automated approach could standardize the
build process, ensuring that every step—from dependency manage-
ment to error resolution—is performed consistently and efficiently.

This would mitigate human error, reduce system downtime, and
fortify the security posture of HPC environments [26, 28].
An automated system could continuously monitor the status
of software builds, verify the integrity of installations, and imme-
diately address any compilation or configuration errors. It would
replace static instructions with dynamic, context-aware interac-
tions capable of adapting to the specific challenges presented by
each software package. For instance, if a particular dependency
fails to compile due to a misconfiguration, an automated system
could detect the discrepancy, adjust the configuration parameters,
and reinitiate the build process without manual intervention. Such
capabilities are particularly valuable in large-scale HPC settings,
where downtime or missteps in the software installation process
can have cascading effects on research productivity and operational
efficiency.
Recent innovations in large language models (LLMs) have opened
new frontiers in complex processes, offering promising solutions to
automate challenging tasks previously thought to require human
expertise [3, 14]. Building on these breakthroughs, researchers have
begun integrating LLM capabilities into collaborative multi-agent
frameworks that enhance decision-making and process orchestra-
tion [20, 30]. LLM-based multi-agent systems offer a promising
solution by leveraging natural language understanding and au-
tonomous reasoning capabilities. In our proposed approach, differ-
ent LLM-agents work in concert to navigate the complex landscape
of software builds. This research makes several contributions to the
field of HPC software management. First, we introduce an approach
for automating the compilation, deployment, and troubleshooting
of HPC software using an LLM-based multi-agent system. Our main
research question is: "To what extent can an LLM-based Multi-Agent
System streamline, automate, and improve the accuracy of software
installation processes compared to traditional documentation and
support methods in HPC environments?" Our approach harnesses
the power of intelligent agents that work in concert to signifi-
cantly reduce the manual overhead and error rates traditionally
associated with software builds. In our framework, various agents
are assigned specialized tasks, such as interpreting technical docu-
mentation, generating build scripts, and iteratively diagnosing and
correcting errors. This division of labor enables the entire process
to be executed more swiftly and accurately, mitigating issues that
commonly arise from human error and trial-and-error methods.
The resulting system is not only more efficient but also provides a
scalable solution that adapts to the challenges inherent in managing
diverse software configurations and complex dependency networks
in HPC environments.
We conducted experiments using Deepseek R1 distilled Llama
8B, Llama 3.1 8B, OpenAI’s ChatGPT 4 and Anthropic’s Claude 3
model within a Linux-based virtual machine in order to validate
our proposed framework. Our experiments spanned 100 distinct
software packages, each subjected to 10 trials to rigorously test
the system’s robustness and reliability. Through quantitative and
qualitative analyses, this work compares lower-cost closed models
(Claude/ChatGPT) and open-source (DeepSeek and Llama) to find
cost-effective solutions for software building automation. These
results highlight LLM-based automation’s capacity to revolutionize
HPC software management by reducing downtime and strengthen-
ing security. Our findings demonstrate autonomous agents’ effec-
tiveness in managing deployment complexities, enabling resilient
systems while evaluating cost-efficient closed and open-source mod-
els. This work addresses critical HPC challenges and establishes
foundations for automating intricate software engineering tasks.
The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 examines automated
software building trends and LLMs’ role in automation. Section 3
details our methodology, including model specifications and the
LLM-based multi-agent architecture for HPC compilation. Section
4 analyzes experimental outcomes, focusing on build success rates
and automated error resolution. Section 5 discusses implications
versus traditional methods and future research paths. Section 6
summarizes contributions and broader impacts on HPC systems.
2
Background
Automated software building is widely sought after in HPC en-
vironments to reduce the burden of system administrators while
increasing the level of automation and software availability on their
systems. This background section provides the state of automated
software building, followed by a description of how LLMs address
similar issues in other similar domains.
2.1
Automated Software Building
Automated software building uses tools and scripts to streamline
software development, including compiling code, deploying applica-
tions, and running tests. In HPC, challenges in software deployment,
system optimization, job scheduling, and user software manage-
ment require efficient software-building mechanisms. Automating
these processes helps developers manage the growing number of
software packages and repetitive tasks.
A proposed solution is EasyBuild, a Python-based framework
that simplifies software installation and maintenance in HPC by
supporting over 250 scientific software packages and allowing cus-
tomization [16]. Another is Spack, introduced by Livermore Na-
tional Laboratory, which uses a unique syntax for specifying con-
straints and ensures seamless dependency resolution across diverse
environments. Spack’s Subspace extension allows HPC facilities to
tailor package complexity levels [4, 11]. Other common tools in soft-
ware automation are CMake, GNU, Autoconf and Automake, and
Lmod, they facilitate efficient compilation, linking, and deployment
across various architectures.
Another approach to managing software installation is Virtu-
alization. Virtualization creates virtual versions of computing re-
sources, improving development efficiency, integrating heteroge-
neous resources, and enhancing system reliability. Pre-built virtual
machines (VMs) allow users to set up customized environments.
Containerization, using tools like Docker and Singularity, offers
an alternative by preparing software containers with specific in-
stallations. Docker containers often outperform VMs in memory-
intensive tasks [6, 18]. Singularity, developed by Lawrence Berkeley
National Laboratory, allows container use without root access and
integrates well with HPC environments, offering near-native per-
formance [17]. Despite advancements, challenges remain, such as
unique HPC system configurations, replicating environments, secu-
rity concerns, and administrative trade-offs. Emerging approaches,

2.2
Large Language Models and Software
Automation
The emergence of LLMs has led to versatile applications beyond
text generation. Early research enhanced LLM abilities with natural
language rationales and in-context few-shot learning, leading to
the Chain of Thought (COT) method, which breaks down multi-
step problems into intermediate steps, improving interpretability
and reasoning across various tasks [31], and the Tree of Thoughts
(ToT) framework represents problem-solving as a structured tree of
logical sentences [32]. Both are frameworks that have investigated
improving the ability of LLMs by enhancing reasoning.
Recent LLM advancements have approached it differently, by
developing task-specific LLMs, resulting in agents. An example is
the Data Interpreter, built for data-centric problems like machine
learning, data analysis, and mathematical problem-solving. It em-
ploys dynamic planning within a hierarchical structure, breaking
down tasks, executing code, and validating results. A hierarchi-
cal graph organizes data science pipelines into manageable tasks,
facilitating effective orchestration. Dynamic plan management ad-
justs plans based on changing data dependencies. Tool utilization
and generation enhance coding proficiency by integrating existing
code snippets and creating custom tools. Automated confidence-
based verification ensures correctness, while experience-driven
reasoning leverages past task experiences for adaptability. Exper-
imental results show the Data Interpreter’s performance in math
problem-solving, machine learning, and open-ended tasks is well
above baselines [15].
Software development also benefits from task-specific LLMs.
ChatDev, an automated software development framework driven
by LLMs and chat-based interactions, revolutionizes traditional
approaches. ChatDev breaks down the development lifecycle into
designing, coding, testing, and documenting, involving designated
roles in sequential tasks. It tackles challenges like code halluci-
nations with thought instruction, role specialization, and version
evolution. Experimental trials with ChatGPT-turbo-16k demon-
strate ChatDev’s efficiency and cost-effectiveness in automating
software development [27].
Integrating cutting-edge natural language processing techniques
into the software deployment lifecycle opens many opportunities,
especially for HPC. By leveraging LLMs, HPC systems can automate
software build tasks and minimize deployment challenges. This pa-
per evaluates to what extent an LLM agent can effectively automate
the software build process for HPC software packages. It examines
one-shot LLMs, LLMs that self-correct after build failures, and a
novel approach using multiple LLM agents collaborating to build
software packages. The goal is to improve HPC software-building
efficiencies and evaluate LLMs’ effectiveness in automating HPC
administrative tasks.
2.3
Multi-Agent Systems for Automation
A multi-agent system in the context of software automation is a
framework that utilizes several autonomous agents to collectively
execute tasks that are often too complex for a single agent to handle
efficiently [9]. In this system, each agent is designed to perform
a specialized function, such as interpreting technical documen-
tation, generating build scripts, diagnosing errors, or managing
dependencies. These agents operate concurrently and are capable
of independent decision-making, yet they work collaboratively to-
ward a unified objective of automating the software compilation
and deployment process [19].
Agents in a multi-agent system collaborate through well-defined
communication protocols and coordination strategies. They share
information about their individual findings, progress, and any prob-
lems they encounter, which allows them to dynamically adjust their
actions based on the unfolding context of the task. For example, if
one agent identifies a specific dependency issue or a build failure,
it can signal other agents to modify their scripts or configurations,
ensuring that the problem is addressed collectively and efficiently.
This iterative process of feedback and adjustment enhances the
overall system’s ability to handle complex, multifaceted tasks by
dividing them into smaller, manageable components while main-
taining a holistic view of the automation workflow [30].
Using a multi-agent system offers significant advantages over a
single-agent approach. One of the primary benefits is the division of
labor, where each agent focuses on its area of expertise, leading to
increased efficiency and a reduction in the likelihood of errors [21–
25]. Also, the distributed nature of multi-agent system improves
system robustness; the failure or inefficiency of one agent does not
jeopardize the entire process, as other agents can compensate for
gaps and maintain operational continuity. Moreover, MAS facilitates
scalability and flexibility, enabling the system to adapt to increasing
complexity and evolving software environments. In this way, a
multi-agent framework enhances the resilience and adaptability
of software automation, ultimately resulting in more reliable and
effective management of software compilation and deployment
tasks.
3
Methodology
While LLMs have found numerous successful applications, one area
yet to be thoroughly explored is their potential to streamline and
automate HPC software-building processes, offering the opportu-
nity for HPC system to save human resources that would have been
directed to software building. The hypotheses of this paper center
on three key assertions:
(1) LLMs can automate software building by leveraging their
proficiency in generating code through text prompts.
(2) LLMs can enhance their ability to self-correct errors, akin to
their performance in code generation tasks;
(3) Employing multiple LLM agents, particularly when provided
with error messages as context for subsequent attempts, can
improve build pass rates.
This section outlines the approach taken to create software-
build agents, covering the utilization of LLMs and the process of
generation, installation, compilation, execution, and verification of
the software.

3.1
Models
For our experiments, we employed the Deepseek R1 distilled Llama
8B model [13], Llama 3.1 8B model, GPT-4, and claude 3 Opus. Those
models are used on the 6 different approaches:
• Deepseek R1 distilled Llama 8B model is a distilled ver-
sion based on the Llama 8B architecture, designed to re-
duce computational overhead while maintaining key perfor-
mance characteristics. This model was directly fine-tuned
on open-source models using a curated dataset of 800,000
samples, an approach designed to transfer advanced rea-
soning capabilities to a more efficient, smaller model. This
distillation process incorporated knowledge from various
base models—including Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Math-
7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Qwen2.5-32B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-
3.3-70B-Instruct—with Llama-3.3 selected specifically for
its slightly superior reasoning performance over Llama-3.1.
As a result, Deepseek R1 distilled Llama 8B becomes well-
equipped to tackle complex tasks in high-performance com-
puting environments, such as generating precise build scripts
and managing intricate dependency configurations. In this
approach, this model is used as a stand alone model through
the multi-agent system defined in the following section.
• Llama 3.1 8B: Llama 3.1 8B is of the class Llama 3, which is the
most advanced family of model from Meta’s AI. Llama3 will
also be used as a stand alone model through the multi-agent
system described below. The model will also be evaluated
through the Repair version that attempts to self-correct its
build mistake up to 10 attempts.
• GPT-4 (ChatGPT 4) is the most well-known and used LLM. It
is closed source and traditionally outperforms all other LLMs
in public benchmarks [17]. This LLM service represents the
latest advancement from OpenAI, boasting multimodal ca-
pabilities that accept both text and image inputs. In addition,
it achieves 67% success rate at one shot code generation.It
is used as stand alone mode, and is evaluated for both its
one shot performance and its Repair version of the intro-
duced ChatGPT 4 model that attempts to self-correct its build
mistakes up to 10 attempts.
• Claude 3 is the latest version of Anthropic’s LLM. This
closed-source model was demonstrated to be one of the best-
benchmarked LLMs on the market [18]. This model rivals
ChatGPT 4 and has been benchmarked as the most versatile
text model produced by Anthropic, particularly excelling
in code generation, achieving 84.9%. Claude 3 Repair is an
enhanced version of the introduced Claude 3 model that
attempts to self-correct its build mistakes up to 10 attempts.
• Llama3.1 8B + Deepseek R1 repair: Aggregation of LLama3
and Deepseek R1.
• GPT4+Claude 3: Aggregation of GPT4- Repair and Claude 3
Repair.
GPT4 and Claude 3 are closed sources, while Llama3 and Deepseek
R1 are open source reasoning models. The goal of using two type
of different model will be to assess how does generative AI with
reasoning compare against traditional n-shot generative LLMs at
native and container-based software building and installation for
high-performance computing.
3.2
LLM-based Multi-Agent System
The multi-agent system used is made possible through CrewAI.
CrewAI is an open-source framework that facilitates coordina-
tion among AI agents by enabling role-based interactions and au-
tonomous functions. It empowers developers to create AI agents
with different roles, goals, and tools. The fundamental components
of CrewAI include Agent, Task, Tool, and Crew, which can be flex-
ibly combined to build multi-agent systems. Supporting APIs in-
tegration such as with OpenAI API , and Ollama which this work
is using. CrewAI offers features such as customized agent roles,
automated task assignment, and dynamic task handling. It is specif-
ically designed to manage complex processes, including multistep
workflows, decision making, and advanced problem solving. The
framework offers autonomy, using intelligent agents to process in-
structions, review scripts, and diagnose errors by helping minimize
manual intervention.
In this work, two agents are created through the framework
with two roles: Generator and Reviewer. The Generator agent role
is to generate a valid docker file based on the software require-
ments. The Generator is given the background of being an expert
in containerization, especially docker best practices, and it is given
the task of creating the docker file that encapsulates the necessary
commands to build and install a given HPC software package. The
Reviewer agent role is to evaluate the generated docker file to en-
sure correctness, efficiency, and security. It’s given a background
of a Senior DevOps Engineer with expertise in containerization
and safe docker practices. The task it is assigned is to review the
generated docker file, ensure it meets the output requirements, and
improve its security and efficiency.
3.3
Execution Framework
While LLM agents can generate code from text prompts, automat-
ing the entire software build process requires a more structured
approach. This work proposes an iterative execution framework,
illustrated in Figure 1, to manage the compilation and deployment
pipeline. The framework involves distinct stages: Configuration,
Generation, Build, and Validation, with a feedback mechanism for
error correction. Each stage leverages the capabilities of the LLM
agents (Generator and Reviewer) to varying degrees. Our compu-
tational experiments primarily evaluate the overall success of this
framework in building HPC software, which inherently tests the ef-
ficacy of the agents in the generation, build, and validation (through
error correction) stages.
3.3.1
Configuration. During the initial configuration stage, the
system defines essential parameters for the software package build.
These parameters act as a template and constraints to guide the LLM
agents during code generation. This structured input helps ensure
relevant responses and mitigates the risk of errors or extraneous
code. Key configuration elements include:
• The target operating system (OS) for the container.
• Specific commands or package managers (e.g., apt, yum) rele-
vant to the chosen OS, which guide the agents in generating
installation steps.

Based on these configurations and the software package name, the
Generator agent (described in Section 3.2) is tasked with producing
an initial Dockerfile.
3.3.2
Generation. In the generation stage, the LLM agents produce
the necessary build and test scripts. The Generator agent receives
the software package name and the pre-defined configurations.
It leverages its knowledge base to generate an initial Dockerfile
and a basic test script to verify the installation. Following this, the
Reviewer agent (see Section 3.2) examines the generated scripts
for correctness, adherence to best practices, and potential security
vulnerabilities. The agents may interact iteratively, refining the
scripts based on the Reviewer’s feedback, before proceeding to the
build stage. This interaction aims to produce a robust script and
a corresponding test case, ensuring the software’s functionality
can be assessed post-compilation, which contributes to the overall
quality assurance.
3.3.3
Build. The generated script is extracted and saved into a file.
The script for the container and the test script are extracted through
the defined format. The extracted script is saved, and executed by
calling a subprocess for the creation of the docker container.
3.3.4
Validation: During this step, the software is validated the
installation of the software. The framework has a Memory that
stores any previous conversations iterations such that they can
serve as context during the next iteration. It is a temporary memory
only available during the compilation and installation of specific
software. It will store the software input, the text generated by the
LLM model, and the installation and testing results. This component
is necessary to enable the LLM agent to self-correct errors. Upon
execution, the subprocess function returns an execution code: the
echoing of the word success/0 signifies a successful execution (zero
errors), while a code of 1/ or the echoing of failure indicates a failure
(at least one error or failed test). If the validation is unsuccessful,
the error information is sent to the Agents for them to review, and
improve. The feedback loop goes on for 10 trials, if all failed then
the installation is judged uncessful. This will help demonstrate that
agent can enhance their ability to self-correct errors.
As seen in Figure 1, the LLM agent will be given a software name
and the requirements, based on the requirements the agents will
generate a docker file, the code will be evaluated for if the docker
file is valid, if valid it will then be saved, with the reasoning of
the agent as well. The docker file will then be executed through
subprocess, which will expect a return code of 0 if the subprocess
was successfully executed without error. If it is executed with error,
the error will then be fed to the agents for them to regenerate the
code based on the feedback. The agents get a defined n numbers of
trials to generate the correct code.
3.4
Software Packages and Experiment
Experiments were conducted on 102 common HPC software pack-
ages to demonstrate the ability of the LLM-based multi-agent sys-
tem to automate the software build process. These software pack-
ages typically involve compiling source code, enabling users to
submit jobs with their own source code and execute them within
the HPC environment. Examples include Python, CUDA, and Ana-
conda. Python is widely used for AI tasks, CUDA enables GPU
utilization, and Anaconda provides a common collection of data
analytics libraries. Such packages require users to interpret doc-
umentation and compile software. Therefore, the experiments fo-
cused on these 102 common packages with widespread use in HPC
systems.
For the experimental setup, all Docker containers were config-
ured to use Ubuntu 22.04 as the base operating system. The LLM
agents were tasked with generating build scripts that would install
the software with root authorization within these containers. Each
software package build was attempted up to 10 times if initial at-
tempts failed, allowing the system to demonstrate its self-correction
capabilities. For the Generator agent, the prompt included the soft-
ware requirements, the expected output format, and an illustrative
example of a Dockerfile for installing Lua. The Reviewer agent
was provided with context defining its focus areas for the review
process.
4
Results
The experiments examine the build effectiveness and self-correction
efficiency of building software packages using six LLM agent config-
urations: Deepseek R1 distilled Llama 8B (referred to as Deepseek
R1), Llama 3.1 8B (Llama 3), GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus (Claude 3),
GPT-4 with repair (GPT4 Repair), Claude 3 with repair (Claude 3
Repair), and multi-agent configurations (GPT4+Claude 3 Repair,
Llama3+Deepseek R1 Repair). Model effectiveness is first evaluated
by the overall pass rate for building 102 software packages in one-
shot attempts, then with self-correcting agents, and finally with
multi-agent self-correcting systems.

4.2
Analysis of Repair Attempts
This analysis compares the average number of attempts required by
the different repair agent configurations to successfully build each
piece of software, with a limit of 10 attempts per LLM model type
within a configuration. For multi-agent models (e.g., GPT4+Claude3),
each model type had up to 10 attempts, allowing for a total of 20
maximum attempts for the pair if the first model type failed all
10 times. Table 4 summarizes the average attempts for successful

When comparing single repair agents, Claude 3 Repair required
slightly fewer attempts on average than GPT-4 Repair. For multi-
agent approaches, the order of models was significant: Claude3+GPT4
Repair (Claude 3 first) required fewer average attempts (3.59) than

that using Claude 3 as the initial algorithm in a multi-agent pair ex-
pedited the discovery of solutions. The open-source repair models
(Deepseek R1 Repair, Llama 3 Repair) and their combination re-
quired notably more attempts on average. All algorithms exhibited
a notable decrease in the likelihood of successful software builds
after exceeding 5 attempts, indicating a common trend in their
performance curve where early attempts are more critical. Despite
Claude3+GPT4 Repair yielding the highest overall build pass rate
(Table 3), it required approximately 0.45 more attempts on average
than the standalone Claude 3 Repair, which was the second-best
algorithm for build pass rate among single agents.
5
Discussion
The experiments supported the hypothesis that LLM agents can
build common HPC software through text generation and automa-
tion. The one-shot GPT-4 approach achieved nearly 55% success-
ful software builds, slightly higher than Claude 3. However, open
source model struggle at one shot generation, with Llama 3 barely
reaching 5 %, and Deepseek R1 performing worse than it. Those
observation imply that close source models are better for software
building and installation. Based on the data, it is determined that
the main failures in installation for the open source models were
the fact that they weren’t targeting the right source code location,
targeting the wrong GitHub repository, or they had mismatch in
dependencies for the software they were trying to build, isssues
closed source models handled much better.
The experiments also supported the hypothesis that iterative
LLM agents yield higher build success rates. All of the repair models
outperformed their one-shot counterparts, with success rates of
90%, 88%, 51%, and 43% respectively. These agents can assess fail-
ures, identify mistakes, and generate new builds, improving success
probability.
Approaches using multiple LLMs and increased repair iterations
were the most successful. Agents using two LLMs had as high as a
98% success rate, with an average of 4.0 attempts for GPT-4 then

Claude 3 (GPT4+Claude3) and 4.5 attempts for Claude 3 then GPT-4
(Claude3+GPT4). The higher success rate of these dual LLM agents
is due to their increased attempt threshold and the ability to exploit
the strengths of multiple models. If one model struggles with a
build, the other may excel, similar to how the Experts of Models
architecture can improve model accuracy.
Automating software builds with LLM-generated scripts, par-
ticularly those requiring elevated privileges (e.g., root access in
Docker), presents significant security challenges. While our Re-
viewer agent vets scripts, sophisticated LLM-generated code can
contain subtle vulnerabilities, making the execution of such code
inherently risky, even in containers. Future work must integrate
robust security measures like static analysis, stricter sandboxing,
and runtime monitoring tailored for LLM outputs. Furthermore,
the specific context of the HPC environment, including shared re-
sources and security policies, influences the risks and requirements
for the software build. Adapting agent prompts and review criteria
to this context, such as enforcing the use of official repositories
or adherence to institutional policies, is crucial. Enhancing such
context-awareness is vital for future research to improve both the
security and reliability of automated builds.
6
Conclusion
This research work demonstrates that an LLM-based multi-agent
system can effectively automate the intricate process of HPC soft-
ware compilation, deployment, and error resolution. By leveraging
state-of-the-art techniques, our approach achieves a 98% success
rate in autonomously building over 102 common HPC software
packages, highlighting both its efficiency and its robustness. The
system not only manages the generation and refinement of build
scripts with minimal human intervention but also actively iden-
tifies and remedies build and test failures through iterative script
modification. In addition to operational improvements, the agents
provide detailed diagnostic feedback and actionable recommenda-
tions when manual intervention is required, thereby significantly
reducing administrative overhead. These results confirm that the
integration of intelligent agents into the HPC environment automa-
tion workflow is a promising pathway to achieve more resilient
and efficient system operations.
Future work will investigate several avenues. One major area of
exploration is the enhancement of our framework by integrating
more advanced language models and expanding the system’s ca-
pacity to handle an even wider range of software configurations
and dependencies. Another area will refine the error detection and
recovery mechanisms further, enabling the agents to adapt dynam-
ically to new challenges and unanticipated failures. Additionally,
deploying and evaluating the multi-agent system in live, production-
scale HPC environments will be crucial to assess its performance
under real-world conditions and workflows. Efforts to strengthen
the security aspects of the automation process, as well as to inte-
grate continuous learning capabilities into the agents, could further
enhance the system’s adaptability and resilience. Overall, these
future research directions aim to build on our current findings and
pave the way for a more robust, scalable, and integrated approach
to HPC software management.

Abstract: High-performance computing (HPC) systems rely on complex soft- ware configurations that are traditionally managed through manual processes, leading to inefficiencies and increased risk of errors. In this paper, we present an LLM-based multi-agent system designed to automate the compilation, deployment, and error resolution of HPC software. Our approach leverages state-of-the-art language models to generate, refine, and iteratively improve build scripts, thereby reducing reliance on static documentation and manual intervention. Extensive experiments on a benchmark cluster demonstrate a 97% success rate in autonomously building over 200 commonly used HPC software packages. Moreover, our agents effectively identify and rectify build and test failures and provide detailed descriptions with actionable recommendations when manual intervention is required. This advancement significantly reduces administrative overhead, enabling HPC administrators to reallocate resources to other critical tasks and paving the way for more resilient and effi- cient system operations.
